title: Plum Island: Competing Claims and a Continuing Montaukett Voice
summary: Wyandanch, Samuel Wyllys, Southold townsmen and English governor Edmund Andros appear in competing claims to Plum Island. The history continues in the Montaukett Indian Nation’s call to participate in decisions about the island’s future.
address_label: Plum Island, off Orient Point — modern main-island outline
map_geometry_source: Modern main-island shoreline, not a reconstruction of the 1659 agreement or1675 patent.
why_this_matters: Who gets to decide what happens to a homeland? Colonial deeds, town divisions, manor authority and federal ownership changed control of Plum Island. The Montaukett Indian Nation’s call for consultation shows why conservation planning must also reckon with Native relationships and authority.
introduction_title: Deeds, colonial authority and a living Native voice
introduction_content: Wyandanch, Samuel Wyllys, Southold townsmen and English governor Edmund Andros appear in competing claims to Plum Island. The history continues in the Montaukett Indian Nation’s call to participate in decisions about the island’s future.
history_content:
A Native island at the meeting of the waters

Plum Island lies just across Plum Gut from Orient Point, at the eastern end of Long Island's North Fork. It is part of a connected landscape of islands, shorelines and travel routes. The existing Manittuwond place-name article provides another entry into that Native geography. The later record of deeds and patents should be read as a history of competing claims over a homeland, not as the beginning of the island's human history.

Wyandanch, Samuel Wyllys and Southold's competing claim

The appendix to Southold Town Records describes an agreement made at Gardiners Island on April 27, 1659 between Wyandanch, spelled Wyandank in that account, and Samuel Wyllys of Hartford. It then traces a separate effort by Southold's English colonial townsmen to treat Plum Island as property they could divide among themselves. A town vote dated March 19, 1665/6 divided the island into shares; the account records transfers of those shares to John Youngs in May 1666. Southold Town Records, volume II

These were competing assertions of authority, not a single uncomplicated transaction. An English town's vote to distribute land and an individual's claim through a Native agreement were different mechanisms. Their coexistence raises the question of who claimed the power to decide the island's future. It does not establish that every Native community with relationships to the island agreed to those claims.

An English governor grants manor authority

The New York Genealogical and Biographical Society's index of manors dates Governor Edmund Andros's grant to Samuel Wyllys to April 2, 1675, citing the original land-patent series. It identifies Plum Island and Great Gull Island and describes the grant as carrying local autonomy. The index therefore points to more than a transfer of acreage: a colonial governor was also conferring governmental authority. Manors in New York (Part Two): Plum Island

The old Southold appendix gives 1674, while the indexed patent date is 1675. The later date is used here with that distinction made explicit. A grant from the English colonial government is evidence of what that government claimed it could authorize; it is not a new agreement signed by Native people. The outline shown here covers modern Plum Island only, not every island named in the patent. Southold Town Records, volume II Manors in New York (Part Two): Plum Island

Private estates became federal land

Historical material submitted to a March 2024 congressional hearing traces another change in control: Abram Hewitt sold land on Plum Island to the United States in installments in 1897 and 1901 for Fort Terry. Military use was followed by the island's animal-disease research role. Those later public uses did not answer the question of Native relationships to the place. A federal facility and a Native homeland are different ways of describing the same island's history. House Federal Lands hearing, March 7, 2024

Who participates in the island's future?

In a statement published July 16, 2026, Sandi Brewster-walker, Executive Director and Government Affairs Officer of the Montaukett Indian Nation, objected to Suffolk County seeking to acquire Plum Island without consulting the Nation. She identified the island as ancestral territory and called for the Nation's participation in decisions about it. Her statement appeared alongside conservation organizations supporting the County's plans. The difference matters: agreement that a place deserves protection does not mean agreement about who should control it or how decisions should be made. Preserve Plum Island Coalition Applauds Suffolk County’s Plan for Plum Island

This is a living discussion about authority, consultation and care for land, not a completed return of the island to Native ownership. Learning about LandBack here means listening to the priorities expressed by the Nation, rather than assuming that a conservation transfer alone resolves dispossession.

Continue with the Manittuwond / Plum Island place-name article and its earlier Historic Moments.
whereintheworld_content: The outline follows modern Plum Island for geographic orientation. It is not a surveyed reconstruction of the 1659 agreement or the 1675 patent. Great Gull Island is named in the patent index but is not included in the shaded area on the map. The map does not establish current legal ownership or public access; it connects a documented land history with an ongoing Native voice.
